overview: This atlas labels one 1492 to 1650 map record 'Bengal,' but it crosses a major change: an independent sultanate gave way, through Afghan and regional resistance, to Mughal provincial government. Bengal was a river delta of shifting channels, farms, market towns and many communities, not a single uniform court. The later imported polygon even misses much of the eastern delta around Dhaka; its outline is a rough source snapshot, not a reliable boundary of Mughal rule.

periods.title: Late independent sultanate
periods.summary: Husayn Shah's dynasty ruled an independent Bengal with courtly inscriptions and regional building.

periods.title: Afghan dynasties and contest
periods.summary: Afghan rulers and Mughal armies contested the delta; its government did not change in one stroke.

periods.title: Mughal conquest, local resistance
periods.summary: The Mughal claim from 1576 took decades to reach resistant eastern districts.

periods.title: Mughal Bengal
periods.summary: Dhaka became a provincial center as rivers connected farms, markets and administrators.

items.text: At the turn of the sixteenth century, the Husayn Shahi court belonged to an independent Bengal sultanate. A stone inscription dated 1500 names Prince Daniyal, a son of Sultan Husayn Shah, as patron of a mosque. Its tall, curling letterforms turn a building record into art. The stone says something about court patronage, not how every village worshipped.

Mughal forces defeated the last independent Bengal sultan in 1576, but control of the delta was gradual. Eastern landlords and rival powers continued to resist, and Dhaka became a Mughal provincial capital in the early 1600s. The map's single name therefore spans different regimes and different degrees of control.

Rivers were routes, not merely lines on a map. The Ganges, Brahmaputra, Meghna and smaller channels carried travel and goods through a changing delta. Moving channels and new fields could alter where people farmed, traded or sought patrons. A solid border drawn across the water hides these local changes.

At Khalifatabad, now Bagerhat, planners built brick roads and bridges alongside mosques and water tanks in the fifteenth century. The reservoirs and drainage show practical work behind a monumental city: people needed water and passable routes as well as places to pray. This is evidence for one town, not a claim that every home had such facilities.

Rice fields spread into parts of the eastern delta as people cut forest, managed wet ground and founded settlements. This took families, cultivators and local organizers, not only orders from a distant king. In the sixteenth century, Bengal rice traveled by sea as far as the Moluccas, Maldives and Goa. A familiar dinner grain could be a far-traveled trade good.

A 1415 visitor described women and men working fields or weaving according to season; a Mughal writer around 1595 reported women managing many public transactions. These are observations by particular outsiders, not a rule for every faith, class or district. They remind us that the work behind food and cloth was not only men's work.

Some Bengal families made textiles for distant buyers. An early seventeenth-century cotton-and-wild-silk embroidery shows mermaids, hunters and figures inspired by foreign pictures. Imagine a cloth worker choosing how to stitch a creature they may have known only from a story or drawing. It was an export piece, not proof that every family owned a mermaid blanket.

A surviving Satgaon coverlet carries European biblical stories, classical myths and a Hindu fish avatar. Portuguese buyers prized such Bengal embroidery, and examples sold dearly in England. Its mixed scenes show makers adapting designs for trade; they cannot tell us what the embroiderers themselves believed or how most Bengali households slept.

In some sultanate-era learning circles, teachers and scholars discussed religious law, logic, mathematics and medicine. A scholarly center at Sonargaon is one example. This tells us what selected institutions taught, not that every child attended school or received medical care. Many skills were also learned through household and craft work.

An original-script transcription of the 1500 mosque inscription includes 'بنی هذا المسجد الجامع شاهزاده دانیال' (approximately, 'Prince Daniyal built this congregational mosque'). The stone is in Arabic using a distinctive Bengal tughra calligraphic style. This is a courtly building text, not an example of the Bengali language spoken in many homes; the online transcription has not been re-deciphered from the stone here.

A university museum preserves another Arabic inscription from Husayn Shah's reign. Stone texts like this belong to a courtly and religious written record; they are not a sample of every person's speech. Bengali was also spoken and written in the region, alongside other languages.

ending.text: The independent Bengal sultanate ended with Mughal victory in 1576, but the conquest of the eastern delta took decades. Bengal's farms, towns and communities continued within the Mughal province well after this map record stops at 1650. Neither 1576 nor 1650 marks the disappearance of Bengali people or culture.
